analysis.subject: computing
analysis.pageCoverage: Page defines big-O notation as an asymptotic upper bound, gives the formal inequality with constants c and k, illustrates with a quadratic example, and compares quicksort and bubble sort growth.

overview.headline: Understanding big-O as an asymptotic upper bound for algorithm growth

keyPoints.point: Students learn that big-O provides a theoretical measure of execution time or memory needed for a given problem size n.
keyPoints.quote: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm, usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n

keyPoints.point: Students learn the formal definition states big-O holds when positive constants c and k bound the function for all sufficiently large n.
keyPoints.quote: Formal Definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are positive constants c and k, such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ k.

keyPoints.point: Students see the example where n² + 3n + 4 is O(n²) since it stays below 2n² for all n greater than 10.
keyPoints.quote: As an example, n² + 3n + 4 is O(n²), since n² + 3n + 4 < 2n² for all n > 10 (and many smaller values of n).

keyPoints.point: Students recognize big-O notation is often misused to mean less than rather than equal to, with Theta expressing equality.
keyPoints.quote: big-O notation is often misused to mean "equal to" rather than "less than".

keyTerms.gloss: Notation for an upper bound that is often misused in place of equal to.
keyTerms.quote: big-O notation is often misused to mean "equal to" rather than "less than".

keyTerms.gloss: Alternative name indicating an asymptotic limit above actual growth for large inputs.
keyTerms.quote: Also known as O, asymptotic upper bound.

keyTerms.gloss: Step-by-step procedure whose execution time or memory is analyzed for a given problem size.
keyTerms.quote: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm, usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n

keyTerms.gloss: Input magnitude given by number of items n that determines time or memory needed.
keyTerms.quote: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm, usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n

keyTerms.gloss: Fixed positive values that make the inequality hold for all sufficiently large n.
keyTerms.quote: there are positive constants c and k, such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ k.
